title: Gravitational Casimir-Polder interaction in a thermal bath
authors: Shijing Cheng, Tianxin Wang, Zili Zhang
abstract: We have investigated, by separating the contributions from thermal fluctuations (tf) and the radiation reaction (rr), the gravitational Casimir-Polder interaction between a gravitationally polarizable two-level object and an infinite gravitational Dirichlet boundary in a thermal bath at a temperature $T$. The results indicate that the rr-contribution to the interaction potential is independent of the temperature, whereas the tf-contribution is generally governed by a nontrivial interplay between the thermal corrections and the polarization effect. Here, the object-to-boundary distance, the characteristic transition wavelength of the object and the thermal wavelength of gravitons are denoted by $L$, $λ$ and $β$, respectively. In contrast to the vacuum case, where the interaction potential scales as $L^{-5}$ for $L\llλ$ and $L^{-6}$ for $L\ggλ$, corresponding to an always repulsive force, qualitatively new behaviors emerge at high temperatures. Particularly, when $\sqrt[4]{βλ^3}\ll L\llλ$ and the object is polarizable within the plane perpendicular to the boundary, a novel scaling of $TL^{-1}$ arises; when $\sqrt{βλ}\ll L\llλ$ and the object is polarizable along the vertical-to-boundary axis, the interaction force becomes surprisingly attractive. At extremely high temperatures and large distances, i.e. when $β\ll λ\ll L$, the potential oscillates with the distance $L$ and thus an attractive or repulsive and even vanishing force can be resulted, depending on the exact values of $L$. Our work demonstrates that thermal gravitons can act as an active control mechanism for quantum gravitational interactions, and temperature, polarization configuration, and object-to-boundary distance jointly determine the magnitude, scaling law, and even the attractive or repulsive nature of the interaction force.
summary: This paper theoretically examines the gravitational Casimir-Polder interaction in a thermal bath by separating contributions from thermal fluctuations and radiation reaction. It reveals that temperature significantly modifies the force's behavior, leading to novel distance scalings and even switching between attraction and repulsion depending on polarization. The findings establish thermal gravitons as a key control mechanism for quantum gravitational forces.
main_problem: The study investigates the gravitational Casimir-Polder (CP) interaction between a gravitationally polarizable two-level object and an infinite boundary placed in a thermal bath.
main_result: Novel behaviors emerge at high temperatures, including non-trivial scaling laws ($TL^{-1}$) and surprisingly attractive forces depending on polarization and distance. Thermal gravitons act as an active control mechanism for these quantum gravitational interactions.
method: The interaction potential is calculated by separating contributions from thermal fluctuations (tf) and radiation reaction (rr), utilizing the DDC formalism and two-point correlation functions in a thermal state.
model_or_system: The system models a two-level object interacting with fluctuating gravitational fields near a Dirichlet boundary, analyzed using weak-field approximations for metric perturbations.
key_observables: Interaction Potential ($\delta E$), force magnitude and sign (attractive/repulsive).
important_parameters: Object-to-boundary distance ($L$), characteristic transition wavelength ($\lambda$), thermal wavelength of gravitons ($ eta=1/T$).
main_assumptions: The object is assumed static, and the analysis relies on separating contributions into $	ext{tf}$ and $	ext{rr}$ components across various limiting regimes (low vs. high temperature).
paper_structure: The paper analyzes the total potential by splitting it into temperature-dependent ($	ext{tf}$) and radiation reaction ($	ext{rr}$) parts, examining specific distance/temperature regimes to reveal novel scaling laws and force behaviors.
why_interesting: This work extends Casimir physics into the realm of quantum gravity and thermal environments, showing how environmental factors (temperature) can fundamentally alter the nature (sign, scaling) of fundamental vacuum interactions.
